Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four. Fortran (formerly FORTRAN) is a third-generation, compiled, imperative programming language designed for numeric computation and scientific computing.
Which of these is an astronomer?
Frank Kameny is an astronomer. Franklin Edward Kameny (May 21, 1925 – October 11, 2011) was an American gay rights activist.
Which of these is a mathematician?
Joseph Liouville is a mathematician. The crater Liouville on the Moon is named after him.
What is the atomic number of Meitnerium?
Meitnerium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Mt and atomic number 109.
What is the atomic number of Rubidium?
Rubidium is a chemical element; it has symbol Rb and atomic number 37.
In what year did Hedy Lamarr die?
Hedy Lamarr (born Hedwig Eva Maria Kiesler; November 9, 1914 – January 19, 2000) was an Austrian and American actress and inventor.
In what year was Eris discovered?
Eris (minor-planet number 136199) is the most massive and second-largest known dwarf planet in the Solar System.
Metronidazole: Pfizer. Metronidazole, sold under the brand name Flagyl and Metrogyl among others, is an antibiotic and antiprotozoal medication.
Gurjar: India. The Gurjar are an agricultural ethnic community, residing mainly in India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan, divided internally into various clan groups.
Who is credited with discovering Microscopium?
Microscopium: Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. The name is a Latinised form of the Greek word for microscope.
Who is credited with discovering Toluene?
Toluene: Pierre Joseph Pelletier. Toluene is a colorless, water-insoluble liquid with a sweet smell, and is partially responsible for the aroma of gasoline and paint fumes.
Who is credited with discovering Pethidine?
Pethidine: Otto Eisleb. Pethidine, also known as meperidine and sold under the brand name Demerol among others, is a fully synthetic opioid pain medication of the phenylpiperidine class.
Who is credited with discovering Polonium?
Polonium: Marie Curie. Polonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Po and atomic number 84.

This Austrian psychotherapist founded a school of psychology emphasizing birth order and belonging, breaking from Freud by proposing that contributing to others is key to a person's sense of worth — who is he?
Alfred Adler (Austrian; February 7, 1870 - May 28, 1937) was an Austrian medical doctor, psychotherapist, and founder of the school of individual psychology.

This American anthropologist specialized in the economic anthropology and rural development of Indonesia, earning her PhD from the University of Hawaii in 1992 after studying women's weaving and blacksmithing on Java. Who was she?
Ann Dunham (November 29, 1942 - November 7, 1995) was an American anthropologist who specialized in the economic anthropology and rural development of Indonesia.
The second-largest living lizard species after the Komodo dragon, native to South and Southeast Asia. It's a varanid found from India to the Indonesian islands. What is it?
Asian water monitor (Varanus salvator) is a large varanid lizard native to South and Southeast Asia.
Six carbons in a flat hexagonal ring, each wearing a single hydrogen — this textbook aromatic hydrocarbon has the formula C6H6 — what is it?
Benzene is an organic chemical compound with the molecular formula C6H6.
Unlike most elements, this one is made almost entirely by cosmic ray collisions rather than inside stars, making it rare despite its light atomic weight. What element is it (symbol B)?
Boron is a chemical element; it has symbol B and atomic number 5.
Produced when quicklime is mixed with water, this white, powdery compound goes by many names in industry and food prep, where it's labeled E526 — what compound is it?
Calcium hydroxide (traditionally called slaked lime) is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula Ca(OH)2.
Sporting one pair of legs per body segment, this venomous arthropod always has an odd number of leg pairs — anywhere from 15 to 191 — what is it?

Centipede (from Neo-Latin centi- 'hundred' and Latin pes, pedis 'foot') are predatory arthropods belonging to the class Chilopoda of the subphylum Myriapoda, an arthropod group which includes millipedes and other multi-legged animals.
In 2023, she became the first woman ever to win the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences on her own, honored for her research on women in the labor market — who is this Harvard economist?
Claudia Goldin (born May 14, 1946) is an American economic historian and labor economist.
This transparent dome covering the iris and pupil provides about two-thirds of the eye's total focusing power and can be reshaped via LASIK surgery — what is it?
Cornea is the transparent front part of the eye which covers the iris, pupil, and anterior chamber.
This progressive, incurable neurocognitive syndrome — often tied to Alzheimer's — brings a decline in memory, thinking and motivation across mild-to-major stages. What is it?

Dementia is a syndrome, often associated with neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, and characterized by a general decline in cognitive processes that affects the ability to perform everyday activities.
Sometimes called word blindness, this learning disability makes reading, writing, or speaking difficult despite a normal desire to learn, and often overlaps with ADHD — name the condition?
Dyslexia is a learning disability that affects either reading, writing, or speaking.
Also known as human herpesvirus 4, this common virus was the first identified oncogenic virus and causes infectious mononucleosis in 90% of cases. What is it?
Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), also known as human herpesvirus 4 (HHV-4), is one of the nine known human herpesvirus types in the herpes family, and is one of the most common viruses in humans.

Patented in 1979 but not used medically until 1996, this second-generation antihistamine treats allergic rhinitis and hives while causing far less drowsiness than older allergy medications — what's the drug?
Fexofenadine is an antihistamine medication used in the treatment of allergy symptoms such as allergic rhinitis and urticaria.

This computer scientist demonstrated a working prototype of his operating system CP/M in 1974 and later founded Digital Research — his invention of the BIOS helped make the personal computer revolution possible. Who is he?
Gary Kildall (May 19, 1942 - July 11, 1994) was an American computer scientist and microcomputer entrepreneur.
Also called the woodchuck, this North American rodent is exceptional among its kin: while most marmots live in rocky mountains, this lowland burrower roams the Eastern U.S. into Alaska — what is it?
Groundhog (Marmota monax), also known as the woodchuck, is a rodent of the family Sciuridae, belonging to the group of large ground squirrels known as marmots.
A member of the human Herpesviridae family, this contagious pathogen comes in two types, with about 67% of people under 50 carrying the first as of 2016. What is it?
Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1 and HSV-2) are two members of the human Herpesviridae family, a set of viruses that produce viral infections in the majority of humans.

Literally meaning 'below mania,' this psychiatric condition brings a non-contextual elevation of mood along with increased energy, irritability, and impulsivity, but without the psychotic features of full mania — name this condition?
Hypomania (literally "below mania" or "less than mania") is a psychiatric condition of abnormally heightened mood and increased energy that is less severe than mania.
Part of the fig and mulberry family and thriving in tropical lowlands, this giant of the produce world can weigh as much as 55 kg and measures up to 90 cm long — what is it?
Jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus) is a species of tree in the fig, mulberry, and breadfruit family (Moraceae).
This mammalogist survived a 3,000-meter fall strapped to her airplane seat after a 1971 lightning strike, then spent 11 days alone in the Amazon before rescue — who is she?
Juliane Koepcke (born 10 October 1954), is a German-Peruvian mammalogist who specialises in bats.
The last member of the actinide series, this synthetic element is named for the inventor of the cyclotron — which element holds atomic number 103?
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lr (formerly Lw) and atomic number 103.

Featuring a distinctive twin-boom design with a central pod housing the cockpit and guns, this American World War II fighter aircraft also served as a night fighter and long-range escort when fitted with drop tanks — which aircraft?
Lockheed P-38 Lightning is an American single-seat, twin-engined fighter aircraft that was used during World War II.
A sugar alcohol used both as a low-calorie sweetener and as a medication to reduce eye and brain pressure. It's poorly absorbed by the intestines. What's the name of this compound?
Mannitol is a type of sugar alcohol used as a sweetener and medication. It is unclear if use is safe in pregnancy.

This chemical compound, typically administered by vein injection, is primarily used to treat methemoglobinemia and was used for over a century against malaria. Common side effects include headache, nausea, and vomiting. What is it?
Methylene blue is a salt used as a dye and as a medication.
A demyelinating disease whose relapsing-remitting form shows up in about 85% of patients, it can cause double vision, muscle weakness, and loss of coordination — what is it?
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks myelin, the insulating cover of nerve cells in the human body, causing damage to one's own central nervous system.

A former director of Russia's FSB intelligence agency, this politician served as Secretary of the Security Council of Russia from 2008 to 2024 and is considered one of Putin's closest advisors — who is he?
Nikolai Patrushev (born 11 July 1951) is a Russian politician, security officer and former intelligence officer who served as the secretary of the Security Council of Russia from 2008 to 2024.
Triggered by repeated tension on the growth plate of the upper shinbone from running or jumping sports, this condition causes a tender bump below the kneecap in teens — what is it?
Osgood–Schlatter disease (OSD) is inflammation of the patellar ligament at the tibial tuberosity (apophysitis) usually affecting adolescents during growth spurts.
Sometimes mistaken for wild pigs, these New World ungulates roam from the southwestern U.S. through Central and South America and into Trinidad — name the family?
Peccary (also javelinas or skunk pigs) are pig-like ungulates of the family Tayassuidae (New World pigs).

This eating disorder involves compulsively craving or eating substances not meant for consumption, and takes its name from the Latin word for a magpie famed in folklore for eating anything — what is it?
Pica (disorder) is the psychologically compulsive craving or consumption of objects that are not normally intended to be consumed.
Domesticated roughly 8,000 years ago in Southeast Asia, chickens are the most common example of this category of farmed birds — what's the term?
Poultry are domesticated birds kept by humans for the purpose of harvesting animal products such as meat, eggs or feathers.

The sole species in its genus within the same plant family as apples and pears, this deciduous tree produces a hard, aromatic golden-yellow fruit that's tart raw but turns into jam when cooked — name the fruit?
Quince (Cydonia oblonga) is the sole member of the genus Cydonia in the Malinae subtribe (which contains apples, pears, and other fruits) of the Rosaceae family.
First created near Darmstadt in 1994 and named for the physicist who discovered X-rays, this extremely radioactive element exists as only a handful of atoms with no practical use — which one is it?
Roentgenium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Rg and atomic number 111.
Before becoming a full-time cartoonist in 1995, this creator of a hit workplace-satire comic strip worked various corporate jobs — who is he?
Scott Adams (June 8, 1957 - January 13, 2026) was an American cartoonist, author, and commentator.
Some of these organisms merge single cells into visible fruiting bodies via chemical signals called acrasins, aiding in the decay of vegetation — what group is this?
Slime mold (British) are a variety of small or microscopic organisms in different groups.
Director of research at Cambridge's Centre for Theoretical Cosmology, he was the Lucasian Professor of Mathematics from 1979 to 2009. Who?

Stephen Hawking (8 January 1942 - 14 March 2018) was an English theoretical astrophysicist, cosmologist, and author who was director of research at the Centre for Theoretical Cosmology at the University of Cambridge.
Every part of this Old World evergreen tree is poisonous except the fleshy red covering around its seed, and it's native across Eurasia and Northwest Africa — what tree species is it?
Taxus baccata is an Old World species of evergreen tree in the family Taxaceae.
A nightshade-family relative of tobacco and the potato, this South American native arrived in Eurasia via the Columbian exchange and is botanically a berry eaten as a vegetable — what is it?
Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is a plant whose fruit is an edible berry that is eaten as a vegetable.
At just 26, this Soviet cosmonaut became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth 48 times solo aboard Vostok 6 in 1963. Who is she?
Valentina Tereshkova (born 6 March 1937) is a Russian engineer, politician, and former Soviet cosmonaut.
This evergreen shrub in the nightshade family, native to the Middle East, North Africa, and the Indian subcontinent, is also known as Indian ginseng or winter cherry — what is its scientific name?

Withania somnifera is an evergreen shrub in the Solanaceae family that is native to the Middle East and North Africa, other African regions, southern Europe, Indian subcontinent, and across Southeast Asia.

Introduced to the British Isles by 1500 and known there simply as 'sycamore,' this wind-tolerant maple from Central Europe can grow to 35 metres and has turned invasive in North America and Australia — which species?
Acer pseudoplatanus: Species of maple tree. It is a large deciduous, broad-leaved tree, tolerant of wind and coastal exposure.
Launched to challenge the Boeing 747, this is the world's largest passenger airliner and the only full-length double-deck jet — which aircraft, unveiled in Toulouse in 2005?
This mushroom genus contains the notorious 'death cap,' responsible for roughly 90% of all fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide — which genus?
Amanita: Genus of mushrooms. The genus is responsible for 95% of fatalities resulting from mushroom poisoning, with the death cap accounting for 90% of fatalities every year.

Multicellular eukaryotes that breathe oxygen and grow from a hollow ball of cells called a blastula, over 1.5 million species in this kingdom have been described by scientists. What are they collectively called?
Animal: Biological kingdom. Over 1.5 million living animal species have been described, of which around 1.05 million are insects, over 85,000 are molluscs, and around 65,000 are vertebrates.
The clinging seed burrs of this plant genus, commonly known as burdock, directly inspired the invention of the hook-and-loop fastener — which genus?

Also called the moon jellyfish, this once-thought-cosmopolitan species was split into roughly 28 separate species in the 2020s and is now known to live only in the north Atlantic and off Argentina — which species?
Aurelia aurita: Species of jellyfish. The species now identified as A. aurita is only found in the north Atlantic and in Argentina, and is not dangerous to humans.
Making up nearly 40% of all known insects with around 400,000 described species, this order is distinguished by front wings hardened into protective cases called elytra — what creatures are these?
Beetle: Order of insects. Over 300 species are used as food, mostly as larvae; species widely consumed include mealworms and rhinoceros beetle larvae.

Despite its name, this African animal's hide actually ranges from brown to grey, and it's distinguished from its 'white' cousin by a pointed, hooked upper lip rather than a wide, square one — which species?
Black rhinoceros: Species of mammal. Although the species is referred to as black, its colours vary from brown to grey.
Nicknamed 'murderer's thumb' or 'stubbed thumb,' this genetic trait gives about 2% of people a short, rounded thumb linked to the HOXD13 gene — what is it?
Brachydactyly type D: Abnormal shortening of the distal part of the thumb.
A cole crop related to broccoli, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts, the heaviest recorded head of this leafy vegetable weighed nearly 138 pounds — what is it?
Cabbage: Leafy vegetable in the flowering plant family Brassicaceae.
This infraorder of decapod crustaceans is the true taxonomic home of what everyone actually calls a shrimp, found in fresh and salt water worldwide — what is it?
The largest part of the brain, this structure houses the cerebral cortex plus the hippocampus and basal ganglia, and works with the cerebellum to control every voluntary action. What is it?
Cerebrum: Large part of the brain containing the cerebral cortex.
This Dutch scientist discovered Saturn's largest moon and invented the pendulum clock, the most accurate timekeeper for nearly three centuries — who is he?
Christiaan Huygens: Dutch mathematician and physicist (1629–1695)
Thought extinct since the age of dinosaurs 66 million years ago, this lobe-finned fish was found alive off the west Indian Ocean, more closely related to lungfish than typical fish — what is it?
A heart disease involving reduced blood flow to cardiac muscle due to buildup of plaque in heart arteries — the most common cardiovascular disease. What is it?
Coronary artery disease: Reduction of blood flow to the heart. Procedures such as percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or coronary artery bypass surgery (CABG) may be used in severe disease.
Named after the bladder because it was first found in urine, this amino acid carries a thiol group that lets it forge the disulfide bonds holding many proteins together. Which amino acid is it?
Cysteine: Proteinogenic amino acid. Cysteine (symbol Cys or C) is a semiessential proteinogenic amino acid with the formula HS−CH2−CH(NH2)−COOH.

Doctors once spotted this endocrine condition by its three Ps — polydipsia, polyuria, and polyphagia, or excessive thirst, urination, and hunger — all tracing back to trouble with insulin. Which disease is it?
Diabetes: Group of endocrine diseases characterized by high blood sugar levels.
Working alongside biochemist Katalin Karikó on nucleoside base modifications, this University of Pennsylvania immunologist shared the 2023 Nobel Prize for enabling COVID-19 mRNA vaccines — who is he?
Drew Weissman: American physician and immunologist (born 1959)
Native to southern India, this ginger-family plant produces the aromatic seeds used in both sweet and savory cooking — what is it, botanically?
Elettaria cardamomum: Species of flowering plant.
This fibromuscular tube carries food from throat to stomach using peristaltic contractions, and its name traces to Ancient Greek roots meaning roughly 'I carry what I ate.' What is it?
Esophagus: Vertebrate organ through which food passes to the stomach.

Derived from a Greek word meaning 'to lead out,' this scholarly practice of critically interpreting a text — often the Bible — also examines its historical background and literary genre — what is it called?
Exegesis: Critical investigation of a text.
From the Latin word for 'tube' or 'pipe,' this medical term describes an abnormal connection between two hollow spaces in the body — what is it?
Fistula: Abnormal connection between two hollow bodily spaces, often organs.
Sold under the brand name Lasix, this loop diuretic treats edema from heart failure and kidney disease and can also cause tinnitus and light sensitivity?

Furosemide: Loop diuretic medication. Furosemide, sold under the brand name Lasix among others, is a loop diuretic medication used to treat edema due to heart failure, liver scarring, or kidney disease.
Caught from contaminated water and common among travelers and children, this parasitic infection causes fatty, sticky diarrhea weeks after exposure — what is it?
Giardiasis: Parasitic disease that results in diarrhea.
The largest and most widespread member of its rosy-pink family, this wading bird ranges from Sub-Saharan Africa to the Mediterranean and Central Asia — which species?

Nicknamed the 'Halloween beetle' in North America for invading homes each October to overwinter, this extremely color-variable insect was introduced there from eastern Asia to control aphids — what species is it?
Harmonia axyridis: Species of beetle. Harmonia axyridis is a lady beetle or ladybird species that is most commonly known as the harlequin, Asian, or multicoloured Asian lady beetle.
The offspring of a stallion and a female donkey, this equine hybrid is the rarer reciprocal cross to the mule and was often mistaken in European folklore for a horse-cow hybrid — what is it?
Hinny: Domestic horse–donkey hybrid. It is the reciprocal cross to the more common mule, which is the product of a male donkey (a jack) and a female horse (a mare).
First made in Belgium in 1956 and sold under the brand names Atarax and Vistaril, this first-generation antihistamine also treats anxiety and insomnia — what drug?
Hydroxyzine: Antihistamine drug. It is used in the treatment of itchiness, anxiety, insomnia, and nausea (including that due to motion sickness).
Symbolized by the '∞' sign and debated by philosophers since ancient Greece, this endless concept was later shown by Georg Cantor to come in different sizes when applied to sets. What is it?
Infinity: Mathematical concept. Infinity is something which is boundless, limitless, or endless.
Working under Tamerlane around 1400, this Persian astronomer and mathematician produced work that mostly never reached Europe and stays largely unpublished — who is it?
Jamshid al-Kashi: Persian astronomer and mathematician (c. 1380–1429)
Fluent in Quechua after being raised in two Indigenous households as a child, this Peruvian novelist and anthropologist became known for his intimate portrayals of Andean culture — who is he?
Named from a Norwegian word for 'small fry of fish,' these shrimp-like crustaceans form a biomass of some 379 million tonnes in the Southern Ocean alone — which creatures?

Krill: Small, shrimp-like crustaceans; order of crustaceans. Krill (Euphausiids) (sing.: krill) are small and exclusively marine crustaceans of the order Euphausiacea, found in all of the world's oceans.
Marked by weariness and a desire to act without the energy to do so, which condition can be a normal response to poor sleep or stress, or a sign of underlying illness?
Lethargy: State of tiredness, weariness, fatigue, or lack of energy.
Predominantly black and white with pink and grey highlights, this small Eurasian bird forms social flocks of six to seventeen outside breeding season and often nests in thorny scrub. What is it?
Long-tailed tit: Species of bird in Europe and Asia.

Discovered in 2005 by the same Palomar team whose haul of big, icy Kuiper-belt bodies pushed astronomers to demote Pluto in 2006, this fourth-largest dwarf planet has a methane-frosted, tholin-reddened surface — what is it?
Makemake: Dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt. Makemake (minor-planet number 136472) is a dwarf planet orbiting the Sun in the Kuiper belt, a disc of icy bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Distinguished by its darker camouflage, conformal fuel tanks, and a two-seat cockpit, this all-weather multirole fighter first flew in 1986 for long-range interdiction missions — what is it?
McDonnell Douglas F-15E Strike Eagle: American all-weather multirole fighter aircraft.

Born from the French Revolution's push to standardize units into the metric system, this scientific field oversees everything from the SI unit system to the labs that keep rulers honest — what is it called?
Metrology: Science of measurement and its application.
Nicknamed 'water warts,' this viral skin infection causes small pink bumps with a telltale dimple in the center and usually clears up on its own within a year — what is it?

Molluscum contagiosum: Viral infection of the skin. Molluscum contagiosum (MC), sometimes called water warts, is a viral infection of the skin that results in small raised pink lesions with a dimple in the center.
Also called flystrike, this parasitic condition occurs when fly larvae infest and feed on the tissue of a living animal — what is it?
An oily alkaloid from nightshade plants like tobacco, it doubles as a potent insect neurotoxin and once served as an insecticide, inspiring the neonicotinoid pesticides — what is it?
Nicotine: Chemical stimulant produced by some plants.
This physics principle states that current through a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage across it, expressed as V equals I times R — what's it called?
Ohm's law: Law of electrical current and voltage. Ohm's law states that the electric current through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage across the two points.
A reactive nonmetal of the chalcogen group, it's the most abundant element in Earth's crust — locked into water, silicates, and rust — and the third-most abundant in the universe. What is it?
Oxygen: Chemical element with atomic number 8 (O)
This hickory species native to the Mississippi River region produces a nut used in praline candy and a famous holiday pie, and is the official state tree of Texas — what is it?
Pecan: Species of nut tree native to the southern USA and northern Mexico.
This branch of linguistics studies how speech sounds are articulated, transmitted as sound waves, and perceived, split into three sub-disciplines — what field is it?
Phonetics: Study of how humans produce and perceive sounds.
Home to cereal crops like wheat, rice, and maize as well as bamboo, this is the fifth-largest plant family on Earth — what is it called?
Poaceae: Family of flowering plants commonly known as grasses.

Detected by receptors in your muscles, tendons, and joints, this sense tells your brain where your body is in space, working alongside vision and balance to keep you upright and coordinated — what's it called?
Proprioception: Sense of self-movement, force, and body position.
Found in notable amounts in capers, red onions, and kale, this bitter-tasting plant flavonol is a popular ingredient in dietary supplements — what compound?
Quercetin: Chemical compound. It is found in many fruits, vegetables, leaves, seeds, and grains; capers, red onions, and kale are common foods containing appreciable amounts of it.

Found in fish, dairy, and meat, this fat-soluble vitamin A derivative is prescribed for xerophthalmia and used topically in anti-wrinkle skincare — but too much during pregnancy can harm the fetus. What is it?

Also called 'German measles,' this vaccine-preventable viral infection is usually mild but can cause severe birth defects — including cataracts and deafness — if a mother catches it early in pregnancy. What disease is it?
Rubella: Human viral disease. Rubella, also known as German measles or three-day measles, is a vaccine-preventable infection caused by the rubella virus.
Caused by the same Group A strep behind strep throat, this childhood illness brings a sandpapery red rash and a bumpy tongue — what is it?
The first woman on Facebook's board, she turned the company profitable as its long-serving COO and founded LeanIn.Org — who is she?
In 1948, this Japanese engineer turned a wooden shack producing bicycle motors into a multinational car and motorcycle manufacturer — who is he?
Soichiro Honda: Japanese businessman. Soichiro Honda (本田 宗一郎, Honda Sōichirō; 17 November 1906 – 5 August 1991) was a Japanese engineer and industrialist.
Shaped roughly like a necktie and made up of the manubrium, body, and xiphoid process, which flat bone protects the heart and lungs at the front of the rib cage?
Sternum: Flat bone in the middle front part of the rib cage.
Closely related to privet and native from southeastern Europe to eastern Asia, which flowering shrub genus, commonly called lilacs, hosts caterpillars like the privet hawk moth?
Syringa: Genus of flowering plants in the lilac family.

This rare chromosomal condition gives affected females four copies of a single chromosome instead of the usual two, and is linked to distinctive facial features and skeletal quirks like incurved pinky fingers — what is it called?
Tetrasomy X: Chromosomal disorder with 4 X chromosomes.
These digits let cats walk in a 'digitigrade' stance, while humans are 'plantigrade,' resting on the soles of their feet instead — what are they?
Nicknamed 'Blinder' by NATO, this disappointing supersonic bomber was still exported to Libya and Iraq, seeing combat against Tanzania and in the Iran–Iraq War — which aircraft?
Tupolev Tu-22: Soviet supersonic heavy bomber.
Native to the wetlands of the Carolinas, this carnivorous plant snaps its jaw-like leaves shut on prey after tiny trigger hairs are touched — which plant?

Venus flytrap: Species of carnivorous plant. It is closely related to the waterwheel plant (Aldrovanda vesiculosa) and the cosmopolitan sundews (Drosera), all of which belong to the family Droseraceae.

In general relativity, this hypothetical region of spacetime is considered the theoretical mirror image of a much better-known cosmic trap — nothing can enter it, though light, matter, and energy may escape. What is this region called?
White hole: Hypothetical object of spacetime. In this sense, it is the opposite of a black hole, from which energy, matter, light and information cannot escape.
Sold under the brand name Ambien, which nonbenzodiazepine 'Z-drug' cuts the time to fall asleep by about fifteen minutes?
The symbol for scandium is Sc. Scandium is a chemical element; it has symbol Sc and atomic number 21.
The symbol for hydrogen is H. Hydrogen is a chemical element; it has the symbol H and atomic number 1.

Which one below is best known as a comedian?
Paul Lynde is a comedian. Paul Edward Lynde (June 13, 1926 – January 10, 1982) was an American comedian, actor, and game-show panelist.
In what year was Will Poulter born?
Will Poulter: William Jack Poulter (born 28 January 1993) is an English actor.
In what year was Brittany Murphy born?
Brittany Murphy: Murphy was born in Atlanta; her parents, Angelo Bertolotti and Sharon Murphy, divorced when she was three years old.
In what year was Howard Hughes born?
Howard Hughes: Howard Robard Hughes Jr. (December 24, 1905 – April 5, 1976) was an American aviator, aerospace engineer, business magnate, film producer, and investor.
In what year was Aubrey Plaza born?
Aubrey Plaza: Aubrey Christina Plaza (born June 26, 1984) is an American actress, comedian, writer, and producer.
In what year was Sofía Vergara born?
Sofía Vergara: Sofía Margarita Vergara Vergara (Spanish: [soˈfi.a βeɾˈɣaɾa]; born July 10, 1972) is a Colombian and American actress and television personality.
In what year was Robin Wright born?
Robin Wright: Robin Gayle Wright (born April 8, 1966) is an American actress, producer and director.
In what year was Meghan, Duchess of Sussex born?
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex: Meghan was born and raised in Los Angeles, California.
